attribution.title: Marble Skill Taxonomy (v1)
attribution.standards: Curriculum standards referenced by the taxonomy have their own upstream licences (see PROVENANCE.md in that repository).
attribution.note: This is a starting point, not a diagnosis. Ages are approximate and the taxonomy is not written for learners with additional needs. Treat prerequisite links as a starting point and use professional judgement.

subject: Computing

topics.ds: Step-by-step instructions for everyday tasks (making a sandwich, brushing teeth); that if instructions are wrong or missing, things go wrong; computers follow instructions exactly
e: Write or describe step-by-step instructions for a simple everyday task
Predict what goes wrong if a step is missing or in the wrong order
Explain that a computer follows instructions exactly — it cannot guess what you meant
topics.p: If {{name}} had to write instructions for making a jam sandwich so precise that even a robot could follow them, could they include every single step?

topics.ds: Follow and describe algorithms that include a sequence of steps, branching (a decision such as 'if it is raining, take an umbrella') and iteration (repeating steps, such as 'hop 3 times')
e: Follow movement instructions that include a repeat (e.g. 'repeat 3 times: step forward, clap') and describe which part was repeated
Follow an algorithm with a decision (e.g. 'If the card is red, put it in the box; otherwise put it on the table') and explain what the decision did
Describe the steps, decision and repeat in a familiar routine, such as getting ready for school
topics.p: In a game like 'If I clap, jump; if I stomp, sit — repeat 5 times', can {{name}} follow the rules and explain the 'if' part and the 'repeat' part?

topics.ds: Use input (key presses, mouse clicks, sensors or typed answers) and branching blocks (if ... then, if ... then ... else) with comparison operators to make a visual program respond to the user
e: Program a character to move left and right when the arrow keys are pressed
Write a quiz question that asks for an answer and uses 'if answer = 12 then say Correct, else say Try again'
Use a comparison such as 'if score > 5' or 'if touching colour red' to change what the program does and explain the condition
topics.p: Can {{name}} make a simple game in a coding app where pressing the arrow keys moves a character, or a quiz that says 'Correct' or 'Try again'?

topics.ds: Use repeat (loop) blocks in a visual program to repeat actions a set number of times or forever, and identify where a loop makes a program shorter
e: Rewrite a program that repeats 'move 10 steps' four times so that it uses one repeat block
Use a repeat block to draw a square with a sprite or robot (repeat 4: move, turn 90 degrees)
Explain the difference between 'repeat 10' and 'forever' blocks with an example of when to use each
topics.p: In a coding app, can {{name}} use a 'repeat' block to make a character draw a square or dance — instead of dragging the same blocks over and over?

topics.ds: Implement a simple algorithm as a visual (block-based) program — a start event, a sequence of blocks, run and observe — in an environment such as Scratch, ScratchJr or a programmable robot app
e: Drag blocks into a sequence so a character moves, speaks and changes costume when the green flag is clicked
Run the program and check that it does what the planned algorithm said
Swap two blocks and explain how the order of blocks changes what the program does
topics.p: Has {{name}} used a block-coding app like Scratch to make a character move and talk — and can they explain what happens if they swap the order of the blocks?

topics.ds: Test visual programs by predicting what should happen, running them, finding where the behaviour differs (bugs) and fixing them one change at a time
e: Predict what a short program will do, run it and compare the result with the prediction
Find and fix a bug in a given program (e.g. a character that turns the wrong way or a loop that repeats too many times)
Explain how they tracked down the bug (e.g. running one part at a time, checking each block against the algorithm)
topics.p: When {{name}}'s coding project doesn't work the way they wanted, do they test it, hunt for the 'bug' and fix it step by step rather than starting over?

topics.ds: Implement a designed algorithm as a visual program combining control structures (sequence, multiple branches with if ... else, repeat until), variables and user input, and test it with planned test cases, refining it until it works for all of them
e: Implement their own algorithm (e.g. a quiz, game or sorting tool) as a visual program using if ... else branches, a 'repeat until' loop, a variable and user input
Write and run test cases with expected results, including unusual inputs (e.g. a wrong answer, a blank answer, the highest score), and record the outcomes
Refine the program after testing and user feedback and explain what each change fixed
topics.p: Has {{name}} built a complete game or quiz in a coding app — planning it first, testing it with tricky answers, and improving it until it works properly?

topics.ds: Create and use variables in visual programs to store and change values — such as a score, a timer, a counter or a user's answer — and use them in conditions
e: Create a 'score' variable in a game that starts at 0 and increases by 1 each time the player catches an object
Store a user's typed name in a variable and use it in a message (e.g. 'Hello Sam!')
Use a variable in a condition (e.g. 'if lives = 0 then game over') and explain what the variable holds at each stage
topics.p: In a game {{name}} made with block coding, can they make a score that goes up each time the player wins a point, and end the game when the lives run out?

topics.ds: Spotting AI in daily life: face unlock on a phone, video recommendations, spelling auto-correct, automatic doors that detect people; technology that seems to 'know' things
e: Identify at least five examples of AI in their daily life
Explain that these technologies use patterns and data, not magic or real thinking
Describe one way AI makes their life easier and one time it might not work perfectly
topics.p: Could {{name}} point out several things they use every day — like auto-correct or face unlock — and explain that these are examples of AI?

topics.ds: What a robot really is — not the sci-fi version; robots in factories, robot vacuum cleaners, robot arms in surgery; that robots follow instructions given by people
e: Describe what a robot is (a machine that follows instructions to do a task)
Name at least three real robots and what they do
Explain that robots are not alive and do not have feelings — they follow instructions people wrote
topics.p: If {{name}} saw a robot vacuum cleaner, could they explain how it's different from a person cleaning — that it follows instructions rather than thinking for itself?

topics.ds: Sorting objects into 'smart' (can sense and respond) and 'not smart' (just sits there); a toaster vs a smart speaker; introduction to the idea that some machines can sense and respond to the world
e: Sort a set of objects into 'smart' (responds to input) and 'not smart' (does the same thing every time)
Explain what makes a smart speaker different from a regular radio
Give an example of a machine that senses something and responds (automatic door, motion-sensor light)
topics.p: Could {{name}} explain the difference between a normal light switch and one that turns on automatically when you walk into a room?

topics.n: Voice Assistants and How They Work
topics.ds: What happens when you talk to Alexa, Siri, or Google Assistant; they listen, try to understand, look up answers; sometimes they get it wrong; they are tools, not alive
e: Describe the steps that happen when you ask a voice assistant a question (it listens, processes words, finds an answer, speaks back)
Give an example of a time a voice assistant might get something wrong
Explain that a voice assistant is a computer program, not a person — it doesn't understand or feel
topics.p: If {{name}} asked Alexa or Siri a question and got a wrong answer, could they explain why the voice assistant sometimes makes mistakes?

topics.ds: How recommendation systems work: YouTube, Netflix, and shop websites track what you click and find patterns; filter bubbles; the difference between helpful suggestions and manipulation
e: Explain how YouTube or Netflix decides what to suggest next
Describe what a 'filter bubble' is (only seeing things similar to what you already like)
Give one benefit and one risk of recommendation systems
topics.p: Does {{name}} understand why YouTube keeps suggesting similar videos to ones they've watched, and could they explain how the recommendation system works?

topics.ds: How computer game characters 'decide' what to do; simple rule-based AI vs learning AI; NPCs, difficulty adjustment; AI as the opponent in chess or board games
e: Explain how a computer opponent in a game decides its moves
Describe the difference between a game character that follows fixed rules and one that learns from the player
Give an example of AI making a game more fun (adjusting difficulty, generating levels)
topics.p: When {{name}} plays a video game against the computer, could they explain how the game's characters 'decide' what to do?

topics.ds: Machines make mistakes; they only know what they've been shown; bad training data leads to bad results; AI is not magic — just maths on data; showing edge cases and failures
e: Give an example of AI making a mistake (voice assistant mishearing, auto-correct error, wrong recommendation)
Explain that AI mistakes happen because of gaps or errors in training data
Describe why AI is not magic — it follows mathematical rules applied to data
topics.p: If an AI incorrectly identified a picture of a muffin as a chihuahua, could {{name}} explain why that kind of mistake happens?

topics.ds: Comparing human and machine capabilities: creativity, empathy, common sense vs speed, memory, repetition; the Turing Test (simplified); what makes humans unique
e: Name at least three things humans are better at than computers (creativity, empathy, common sense)
Name at least three things computers are better at than humans (speed, memory, repetitive tasks)
Describe the Turing Test in simple terms (can a computer fool a person into thinking it's human?)
topics.p: Could {{name}} explain what humans are still better at than computers and what computers can do that humans can't?

topics.ds: How machine learning works at a conceptual level: show the computer many examples, it finds patterns, then it makes predictions about new things; hands-on experience with Teachable Machine or similar tool
e: Describe the three steps of machine learning in simple terms (give examples, find patterns, make predictions)
Train a simple model using a tool like Teachable Machine and describe what happened
Explain why showing more and better examples makes the model more accurate
topics.p: Could {{name}} describe how you teach a computer to recognise something — by showing it lots of examples until it spots the pattern?

topics.ds: Humans are great at spotting patterns; computers can learn to spot patterns too, but they need lots of examples; sorting and classification activities as the basis of machine learning
e: Sort a set of items into categories and explain the rules they used
Explain that computers learn patterns by looking at many examples
Describe why a computer needs more examples than a human to learn the same pattern
topics.p: If you showed {{name}} pictures of cats and dogs, could they explain how a computer could learn to tell them apart — and why it would need many more pictures than a person would?

topics.ds: What data AI systems collect about you; who has it and why it matters; cookies, tracking, smart speakers always listening; your data is valuable
e: Name at least three types of personal data that AI systems collect
Explain why personal data is valuable to companies
Describe one step they can take to protect their privacy online
topics.p: Does {{name}} understand that apps and websites collect information about what they do online, and could they explain why that matters?

topics.ds: Deepfakes, AI-generated images and text; how to spot them and why they matter; the importance of checking sources; not everything online is real
e: Explain what a deepfake is and give an example of AI-generated content
Describe at least two clues that might reveal an image or text was AI-generated
Explain why it matters that AI can create realistic fake content
topics.p: If {{name}} saw an amazing photo online, would they think to question whether it might have been created by AI rather than captured by a camera?

topics.ds: Whether AI should make important decisions about people: jobs, loans, justice; who is responsible when AI makes unfair decisions; introduction to algorithmic fairness
e: Give an example of an important decision that AI might help make (hiring, medical diagnosis, loan approval)
Explain why letting AI make decisions about people can be risky if the system is biased
Suggest who should be responsible if an AI system makes an unfair decision
topics.p: If {{name}} learned that a computer program was deciding who gets a job interview, could they explain why that might be unfair and who should be responsible?

topics.ds: AI needs huge amounts of energy and water to train; data centres and their environmental cost; but AI can also help — predicting weather, monitoring deforestation, optimising energy; trade-offs
e: Explain that training AI models uses a lot of electricity and water
Give at least two examples of AI being used to help the environment
Describe the trade-off between AI's environmental cost and its environmental benefits
topics.p: Could {{name}} explain that AI needs a lot of energy to work but can also be used to help protect the environment, and discuss whether the trade-off is worth it?

topics.n: AI and the Future of Work
topics.ds: How AI is changing the world of work: some jobs disappear, new ones are created, many change; jobs AI can't do (yet); what skills matter in an AI world
e: Name at least two jobs that AI is changing or replacing and two new jobs AI has created
Explain why creativity, empathy, and problem-solving are skills that matter more in an AI world
Describe how AI might change a specific job they know about (teacher, doctor, farmer) without replacing it
topics.p: Could {{name}} explain how AI might change the way people work in the future and which human skills will still be important?

topics.ds: If training data is biased, AI will be biased; examples: facial recognition working better for some skin tones, translation assuming gender; where bias comes from and whether we can fix it
e: Explain what bias in AI means using a real-world example
Describe how biased training data leads to biased AI results
Suggest one way to reduce bias in an AI system (use more diverse data, test with different groups)
topics.p: Could {{name}} explain why an AI trained mostly on photos of light-skinned faces might not work as well for people with darker skin?

topics.ds: Design thinking applied to AI ethics: if you were designing an AI system, what rules would you give it? Who should it help? What should it not be allowed to do?
e: Propose at least three rules for a hypothetical AI system they are designing
Explain why AI designers need to think about who might be harmed, not just who benefits
Describe one real example of AI being used responsibly and one where it was not
topics.p: If {{name}} was designing an AI assistant for their school, could they think of rules to make sure it was fair and helpful for everyone?

topics.ds: What AI might do in 10 years; what we want it to do and what we're worried about; children as future designers and decision-makers about AI; hopeful, empowered framing
e: Describe at least two ways AI might be used in the future that don't exist yet
Explain one thing they would want AI to do and one thing they would want it not to do
Describe why it matters that young people understand AI — because they will shape how it is used
topics.p: Could {{name}} have a thoughtful conversation about what they'd want AI to do in the future and what they'd be worried about?

topics.ds: What data is: information that computers use — numbers, words, pictures, sounds; everything a computer knows comes from data that people give it
e: Define data as information stored in a computer (numbers, text, images, sounds)
Give at least three examples of data they create every day (photos, messages, search queries)
Explain that a computer only knows what it has been given — it has no knowledge of its own
topics.p: Could {{name}} explain what 'data' means and give examples of data they create every time they use a phone or computer?

topics.ds: Explain how digital systems represent all data — text, images and sound — using numbers: each pixel's colour is stored as numbers, each letter has a number code and sound is stored as a series of number samples
e: Colour a pixel grid from a list of numbers (e.g. 0 = white, 1 = black) to reveal a hidden picture
Encode a short word using a number code for letters (e.g. A = 65, B = 66 in ASCII) and decode a partner's word
Explain how a photo, a text message and a song are all stored as numbers in a device
topics.p: Does {{name}} know that a photo on your phone is really stored as numbers — and could they turn a list of numbers into a picture on squared paper?

topics.ds: Explore how digital systems represent data using two states — on and off, written as 1 and 0 — called bits, and use binary numbers to represent whole numbers and letters
e: Show every number from 0 to 31 using five binary cards (16, 8, 4, 2, 1) turned face up for 1 and face down for 0
Convert binary numbers such as 1010 and 10011 to ordinary numbers and back
Explain why computers use two states (a switch, light or current is either on or off) and show a letter as a string of bits using a given code
topics.p: Playing with 'binary cards' or light switches, could {{name}} show how on and off (1 and 0) can make any number — like making 5 with 101?

topics.ds: Discuss how existing digital systems satisfy the identified needs of known users: what the user needs, which features help and what does not work well for them
e: List two needs of a known user (e.g. a younger sibling learning letters needs big buttons and sounds)
Explore an existing app or device and point out the features that meet each need
Say one way the system does not suit the user and suggest a change
topics.p: Could {{name}} look at a learning app a younger cousin uses and explain what makes it good for a little kid — like big buttons and sounds — and what could be better?

topics.ds: Investigate simple problems for people they know (classmates, family, the teacher) and suggest how a digital system could help solve them
e: Ask a known user (e.g. a classmate, grandparent or teacher) about something they find hard and record it with pictures or words
Suggest a digital system that could help (e.g. a timer app for taking turns, a video call to see a faraway relative, a talking book for a younger sibling)
Explain how the digital system would solve the problem for that person
topics.p: Can {{name}} notice a problem someone in the family has — like Grandma missing them — and suggest a device or app that would help, like a video call?

topics.ds: Discuss how existing digital solutions and their own digital solutions satisfy the design criteria and user stories, using evidence from trying them out
e: Try an existing app or game against a checklist of design criteria and user stories and record which are met
Test their own program or digital product with a classmate and record which user stories it satisfies
Discuss one criterion or user story that is not yet met and suggest a change
topics.p: After making a game or animation, can {{name}} check it against the goals they set — like 'it must have 3 levels' — and say what still needs fixing?

topics.ds: Define a problem to be solved with a digital solution using given design criteria, and co-create user stories in the form 'As a ..., I want ..., so that ...' to describe what users need
e: Restate a given digital design task (e.g. a quiz game to help Year 1 students learn sight words) as a problem with the given criteria listed
Co-create at least two user stories with a group or a real user (e.g. 'As a Year 1 student, I want to hear each word read aloud, so that I can check I said it correctly')
Check that each user story names the user, what they want and why
topics.p: If {{name}} was helping design a game for younger kids, could they write a 'user story' like 'As a 6-year-old, I want big buttons so that I can tap them easily'?

topics.ds: Generate, communicate and compare designs for a digital solution — sketching or storyboarding the screens, inputs, outputs and steps of a game, app or program — and choose the design that best meets the criteria
e: Sketch two different storyboards for a simple game or animation showing each screen, what the user does and what happens
Present a design to a partner, explaining its inputs, outputs and steps
Compare the two designs against the design criteria and user stories and choose one with reasons
topics.p: Before coding a game, does {{name}} sketch out the screens and what happens when you press each button — and compare a couple of ideas to pick the best?

topics.ds: Design a user interface for a digital system — the layout of screens, buttons, menus and navigation — applying principles such as consistency, readability and accessibility for the intended users
e: Draw wireframes for at least three connected screens of an app or game, showing buttons, menus and how the user moves between screens
Apply interface principles such as consistent button positions, readable text, clear icons and colour contrast, and explain each choice
Test a paper or digital prototype of the interface with a user and note where they got stuck
topics.p: If {{name}} designed the screens for an app, would they think about where the buttons go, how users move between screens and whether it's easy for everyone to use?

topics.ds: Evaluate existing digital solutions and their own against design criteria and user stories, and consider their broader community impact: who benefits, who might be excluded, and effects on privacy, safety, wellbeing and the environment
e: Evaluate their own digital solution against each design criterion and user story using test results and user feedback, rating how well each is met
Evaluate an existing digital solution (e.g. a school app or community website) against criteria they set
Explain the broader community impact of one solution, including who benefits and who could be left out or harmed, and suggest an improvement
topics.p: Can {{name}} judge an app — their own or a real one — against the goals it was meant to meet, and think about who in the community it helps or leaves out?

topics.ds: Generate, modify, communicate and evaluate designs for digital solutions — algorithms, flowcharts, storyboards and wireframes — refining them in response to feedback and testing
e: Generate a design for a digital solution using a flowchart for the algorithm and a storyboard or wireframe for the screens
Communicate the design to users or peers in an annotated presentation and collect feedback
Modify the design in response to feedback and evaluate the new version against the design criteria, explaining what improved
topics.p: When {{name}} plans a digital project, do they share their design, take on feedback and improve it — explaining why the new version is better?

topics.ds: Define problems for digital solutions by creating their own user stories for different users and co-developing measurable design criteria from them
e: Interview or survey intended users and write user stories for at least two different users of a planned digital solution
Co-develop design criteria from the user stories (e.g. 'A new user can sign up in under one minute') and agree how each will be checked
Write a problem statement that combines the users, their needs and the design criteria
topics.p: Before making an app or game, could {{name}} talk to the people who'll use it and turn what they need into clear goals the design must meet?

topics.ds: Identifying computers in everyday life — not just laptops but phones, tablets, smart speakers, traffic lights, washing machines; what makes something a computer
e: Point out at least five everyday objects that contain computers
Explain what all computers have in common (they follow instructions and process information)
Sort a set of objects into 'contains a computer' and 'does not contain a computer'
topics.p: Could {{name}} look around your home and point out at least five things that have a computer inside them, including ones that don't look like traditional computers?

topics.ds: Recognise that digital systems are made of hardware (the parts you can touch, such as the screen, buttons and camera) and software (the apps and programs that tell the hardware what to do), and explore a device or app to achieve a simple purpose
e: Point to two hardware parts of a tablet or computer (e.g. the screen and the camera) and name an app on it as software
Use a tablet app with adult guidance for a purpose, such as taking a photo of a class pet or playing a counting game
Say what the device helped them do and which part or app they used
topics.p: When {{name}} uses a tablet, can they tell you which parts are hardware they can touch (like the screen or camera) and which are apps — and use one app to do something, like take a photo?

topics.ds: Identify the components of common digital systems — screen, keyboard, mouse or trackpad, touchscreen, speakers, microphone and camera — and explore what each is used for, telling parts that put information in (input) from parts that give information out (output)
e: Label the screen, keyboard, mouse or trackpad, speaker, microphone and camera on a picture of a laptop or tablet
Use the microphone to record their voice and the speaker to play it back, saying which part takes sound in and which gives it out
Choose the component they would use for a task (e.g. the camera for a photo of a plant, the keyboard to type their name) and explain why
topics.p: Can {{name}} name the parts of a laptop or tablet — keyboard, screen, camera, microphone, speaker — and say which one they'd use to record a message for Grandma?

topics.ds: Explore and describe a range of digital systems (computers, tablets, game consoles, smart watches, robots) and the peripherals that connect to them — printers, scanners, headphones, game controllers, external drives, digital microscopes and sensors — and choose peripherals for different purposes
e: Connect and use at least two peripherals at school (e.g. headphones and a printer, or a digital microscope) and describe what each adds to the system
Sort peripherals into input, output and storage devices and justify each choice
Recommend a digital system and peripherals for a purpose (e.g. making a class podcast or recording weather data) and explain the choice
topics.p: If the family wanted to record a podcast or print photos, could {{name}} explain which devices and add-ons you'd need — like a microphone, headphones or a printer — and why?

topics.ds: Explore how different types of data — text, images, sound and video — are transmitted between digital systems by cable or wirelessly (e.g. Bluetooth, Wi-Fi, mobile networks), noticing that larger files such as videos take longer to send
e: Send a photo from a tablet to a printer or another device (by cable or wirelessly) and describe the path the data took
Compare sending a text message, a photo and a short video and explain which takes longest and why
Identify whether familiar connections are wired or wireless (e.g. a USB cable, Bluetooth headphones, school Wi-Fi) and give one advantage of each
topics.p: When {{name}} sends a photo or video to a relative, can they explain how it gets there — by cable, Bluetooth or Wi-Fi — and why a video takes longer to send than a message?

topics.ds: Examine how digital systems connect to form networks — wired and wireless connections, routers and servers in a home or school network — so they can share data and resources such as printers, files and the internet
e: Draw a diagram of the school or home network showing devices, the router and wired and wireless links
Explain how a network lets devices share data and resources (e.g. printing from any classroom computer, saving to a shared drive)
Compare a wired and a wireless network connection for speed, reliability and convenience
topics.p: Can {{name}} explain how all the devices at home connect through the Wi-Fi router — and why you can print from any computer in the house?

topics.ds: Explain that the internet is a network of networks and that data is broken into small packets, addressed, sent along different routes and reassembled at its destination
e: Explain that the internet connects millions of smaller networks around the world
Act out sending a message as packets: split a sentence into numbered cards, pass them by different routes and reassemble them in order
Describe what happens when a packet is lost or arrives late (e.g. a video call freezes) and how numbering helps rebuild the message
topics.p: Could {{name}} explain why a video call sometimes freezes — that the internet chops data into little packets that travel separately and are put back together?

topics.ds: Investigate the main internal components of common digital systems — processor (CPU), memory (RAM), storage, circuit board, battery or power supply and wireless adaptor — and explain the function of each
e: Identify the processor, memory, storage and battery in a photo or teardown of a computer, tablet or phone
Explain the job of each part using an analogy (e.g. the processor does the work, memory is the desk for things in use, storage is the cupboard for files)
Compare two devices' specifications (e.g. storage size and memory) and explain how they affect what each device can do
topics.p: Looking at the specs of a new tablet or laptop, could {{name}} explain what the processor, memory and storage each do — and why more storage means more room for photos and games?

topics.ds: Use the basic features of common digital tools to share content and work together — posting a drawing or recording to a class space, adding to a shared class book or slideshow, giving kind comments — following agreed behaviours with guidance from trusted adults
e: Share a photo, drawing or voice recording to a class learning space with teacher guidance
Add their own page or slide to a shared class book without changing anyone else's work
Leave a kind, helpful comment on a classmate's shared work following the class's agreed online behaviours
topics.p: With a teacher or parent helping, can {{name}} add their page to a shared class book or post a drawing online — and leave a kind comment on someone else's work?

topics.ds: Use the core features of common digital tools to share content, plan tasks and collaborate — co-editing a shared document or slideshow, using comments and a shared task list — following agreed behaviours with support from trusted adults
e: Co-edit a shared document or slideshow with group members, each working on an agreed section
Use comments or suggestions to give feedback instead of deleting a classmate's work
Plan a group task in a shared digital checklist or table showing who does what and by when
topics.p: Has {{name}} worked on a shared document or slideshow with classmates — each doing their own part and leaving comments rather than deleting others' work?

topics.ds: Save, name and organise digital files in folders following agreed conventions, so that work can be found, shared and reopened
e: Save a piece of work with a meaningful file name following the class convention (e.g. 'Mia_Y4_Frogs_Report')
Create a folder for a topic, move related files into it and find a file again in a later lesson
Follow other agreed conventions for digital work, such as giving image sources, using a consistent heading style and saving a new version instead of overwriting
topics.p: Can {{name}} save their school work with a sensible file name in the right folder — and find it again the next week?

topics.ds: Select and use appropriate digital tools effectively to create, locate and communicate content — choosing between word processing, presentation, spreadsheet, graphics, video and search tools for a task, using their digital-specific features and applying common conventions
e: Choose the best tool for three tasks (e.g. a budget, a poster, a how-to video) and justify each choice
Use digital-specific features effectively, such as styles and templates, image cropping, spreadsheet formulas or search filters
Apply common conventions such as consistent formatting, file naming, alt text for images and acknowledging sources
topics.p: When {{name}} has a school project, do they pick the right tool — slides for a talk, a spreadsheet for numbers, a video app for a how-to — and use its features well?

topics.ds: Select and use appropriate digital tools to share content online, plan tasks and collaborate on projects — task boards, shared calendars, co-edited documents, version history and video calls — demonstrating agreed behaviours
e: Choose and justify tools for a group project (e.g. a task board to plan, a shared document to write, a video call to meet)
Plan the project in a digital tool with tasks, owners and deadlines and update progress as work is done
Use version history or comments to track and resolve changes, and share the finished project online safely and respectfully
topics.p: For a group project, can {{name}} choose sensible online tools — a shared document, a to-do board, a video call — and use them to plan who does what and keep track?

topics.ds: Identify some data that is personal and belongs to them — their name, age, birthday, address, photos and videos of themselves, voice recordings and drawings — and know to ask a trusted adult before sharing it
e: Sort picture cards into 'about me' (name, birthday, address, a photo of me) and 'not about me' (the weather, a picture of a tree)
Name two things they made that belong to them (e.g. a drawing or a voice recording on a tablet)
Say who they ask before sharing their name or photo on a device (a trusted adult)
topics.p: Does {{name}} know that their name, birthday, address and photos are their own information — and that they should ask you before sharing them in a tablet game?

topics.ds: Discuss that some websites and apps store their personal data online — names, photos, voice recordings, game scores and location — so the information stays there and may be seen by others
e: Name personal data a familiar app or game asks for or keeps (e.g. a username, a photo, a score, a location)
Explain that this data is stored on computers far away (online), not just on their own device
Discuss with a trusted adult whether an app really needs the data it asks for before agreeing
topics.p: When a game or app asks for {{name}}'s name, photo or location, do they understand it gets saved online somewhere — and check with you before typing it in?

topics.ds: Access their school or learning account using a recorded username and password (e.g. from a login card), log out when finished, and keep the password private except from trusted adults
e: Log in to their school account using the username and password on their login card
Log out at the end of a session and explain why (so no-one else can use their account)
Explain that a password is like a key and is only shared with a trusted adult such as a parent or teacher
topics.p: Can {{name}} log in to their school learning app using the username and password on their card, and log out when they're finished?

topics.ds: Access their school account using a memorised password and explain why a good password is easy for them to remember but hard for others to guess, avoiding names, birthdays and simple patterns
e: Log in to their school account from memory without a login card
Sort example passwords into weak (e.g. 'password', 'ben2015', '1234') and strong (e.g. 'purple-kangaroo-jumps') and explain what makes each easy or hard to guess
Explain why a password must be easy for them to remember but hard for others to guess
topics.p: Can {{name}} log in to their school account from memory — and explain why their pet's name or birthday would make a bad password?

topics.ds: Identify what personal data is stored and shared in their own online accounts (e.g. a school learning account or a game) — profile name, photo, age, location, contacts and work — who can see it, and discuss the associated risks
e: Explore the profile and settings of a school or game account with a teacher and list the personal data it stores
Identify who can see each item (only me, my teacher, my class, anyone) and change one privacy setting with adult support
Discuss a risk of sharing data such as a location or full name in a public profile and how to reduce it
topics.p: Looking at {{name}}'s game or school account together, could they tell you what personal information it stores, who can see it and what the risks might be?

topics.ds: Explain how their digital footprint is created — posts, photos, comments, searches and data collected by apps — and why it can be permanent, because content can be copied, shared and stored even after it is deleted
e: List the parts of their digital footprint from one day (e.g. a search, a game score, a comment, a photo a family member uploaded)
Explain why deleting a post does not guarantee it is gone (others may have copied or shared it, and services keep backups)
Decide whether to post a given photo or comment by thinking about who might see it in five years and justify the choice
topics.p: Before posting something online, does {{name}} think about the fact that it could be copied and stay around for years — even if they delete it?

topics.ds: Consider privacy when collecting data from users: collect only the data needed, tell people why it is collected, ask permission, avoid identifying details where possible, and store and share results safely
e: Review a draft class survey and remove questions that collect unnecessary personal data (e.g. full name, address)
Write a short privacy note for a survey explaining what data is collected, why and who will see it, and ask for permission
Explain how to keep survey results private (e.g. share only totals, store them in a protected folder)
topics.p: If {{name}} made an online survey for their class, would they only ask for what they need, explain why, and keep people's answers private?

topics.ds: Access multiple personal accounts using a unique passphrase for each, and explain the risks of reusing passwords: if one account is breached, every account with the same password is exposed
e: Create a passphrase from three or four random words (e.g. 'violin-cactus-ocean-ladder') and explain why its length makes it hard to guess
Log in to at least two different accounts (e.g. a school account and a learning app), each with its own passphrase
Explain what could happen if they used the same password for every account and one website was hacked
topics.p: Does {{name}} use a different passphrase for each of their accounts — and can they explain why reusing one password is risky if a website gets hacked?
